title: What Is Greaseweazle Controller? — Definition
body:
Storage media are the physical carriers of digital (and pre-digital) data: punched cards and paper tape, magnetic drums and tapes, floppy disks, hard disks, optical discs, and the drives that read them. Each generation traded capacity, speed, and cost — from 80 bytes on a punched card to gigabytes on a Jaz disk — and each left behind drives, formats, and data that archivists still rescue today.

In the context of this database, the Greaseweazle Controller is presented as one storage media record among the storage media family. Open-source flux-level floppy interface; the affordable KryoFlux alternative.

title: Origins and History of Greaseweazle Controller
body:
The Greaseweazle Controller belongs to the 2019–present era and traces to Keir Fraser.

Hollerith's 1890 census punched cards mechanized data; IBM's 80-column card (1928) ruled for 50 years. Magnetic tape (UNISERVO, 1951; IBM 729) gave bulk storage; IBM's RAMAC 305 (1956) gave random access with fifty 24-inch platters holding 5 MB. The 8-inch floppy (1971) shrank storage to a desk; 5.25-inch (1976) and 3.5-inch (1981) shrank it to a shirt pocket. Winchester sealed drives (1973) made hard disks reliable; ST-506 (1980) made them cheap. The 1990s brought removable bulk: SyQuest, Bernoulli, Zip, Jaz, magneto-optical, and tape formats (QIC, DAT, DLT, Travan) fighting for backup. Optical (CD-R, DVD) then flash ended the removable-magnetic era — leaving archivists with drives to maintain and disks to image.

Within that longer story, Greaseweazle Controller: F1/F7 boards; writes as well as reads — preservation for the masses. The retro community's imaging workhorse.

title: How Greaseweazle Controller Works
body:
Magnetic storage writes bits as magnetized spots: a head flies microns above a spinning oxide surface (floppy, hard disk) or presses against moving tape. Floppies and early hard disks address data by cylinder/head/sector (CHS); the controller translates to linear block addresses (LBA) on later drives. Punch cards encode characters as hole combinations in 80 columns; paper tape as 5–8 channels across its width. Optical discs read pits and lands with a laser. All removable media share an enemy list: magnetic decay, binder breakdown ('sticky-shed'), mold, and format obsolescence.

Applied to the Greaseweazle Controller (2019–present, Keir Fraser): The retro community's imaging workhorse.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Anatomy of Greaseweazle Controller — Components
body:
Every Greaseweazle Controller is an assembly of the storage media family's standard parts:

• Magnetic head — Read/write transducer; flying, contact, or tape head.
• Spindle motor — Spins disk or capstan at precise speed (300/360 RPM floppy).
• Stepper / voice coil — Positions heads: stepper (floppy) or voice-coil (hard disk).
• Controller — MFM/RLL/ESDI/SCSI/IDE logic translating requests to head motion.
• Jacket / cartridge — Protective shell; the 3.5-inch shutter is iconic.
• Magnetic coating — Iron oxide, chromium dioxide, barium ferrite, metal particle.
• Index hole / sensor — Marks rotation start for timing.
• Write-protect tab — Physical interlock against overwrites.
• Tape transport — Capstan, pinch roller, tension arms in tape drives.
• Laser pickup — Optical head for CD/DVD/MO media.

When examining a surviving Greaseweazle Controller, identify these parts in order: Magnetic head, Spindle motor, Stepper / voice coil, Controller, Jacket / cartridge, Magnetic coating.

title: Storage Media Glossary
body:
The working vocabulary of storage media:

• CHS — Cylinder-Head-Sector addressing; the geometry BIOSes understood.
• LBA — Logical Block Addressing; flat sector numbering replacing CHS.
• MFM / RLL — Encoding schemes; RLL packed ~50% more bits than MFM.
• formatted capacity — Usable space after formatting overhead (e.g., 1.44 MB HD floppy).
• seek time — How fast heads move; milliseconds that defined drive generations.
• sticky-shed syndrome — Binder hydrolysis making old tapes gummy; bake at ~50 C to recover.
• bit rot — Magnetic decay scrambling bits over decades.
• disk image — Bit-for-bit copy (IMG, D64, KryoFlux stream) preserving the original.
• KryoFlux — Forensic floppy controller imaging disks at flux-transition level.
• write once — CD-R/DVD-R: dye layer burned permanently by laser.
• servo track — Factory-written positioning info on hard disks.
• interleave — Sector ordering to match controller speed; 3:1 common on early PCs.

title: Greaseweazle Controller in Culture
body:
Storage media are archaeology you can hold: card decks rubber-banded in attics, shoeboxes of floppies, the Zip disk that ate your thesis. 'Do not fold, spindle, or mutilate' is a cultural punchline. Archivists race bit rot with KryoFluxes; the demoscene still ships on 3.5-inch disks. Every 'save' icon on Earth is a floppy disk most users never touched.

The Greaseweazle Controller carries that cultural charge directly: The retro community's imaging workhorse.

title: Collecting and Preserving Greaseweazle Controller
body:
Unopened floppy boxes, odd formats (3-inch, Floptical, PD), and working drives (especially 8-inch and KryoFlux-compatible) are the prizes. Tape needs baking knowledge; buy from climate-controlled sellers. Keep magnets, heat, and humidity away. Image everything on arrival — media dies, images live.

For the Greaseweazle Controller specifically: Open-source flux-level floppy interface; the affordable KryoFlux alternative.. Prioritize completeness and originality over shine; a working Greaseweazle Controller with honest wear outranks a polished non-runner.

title: Greaseweazle Controller Restoration Guide
body:
Clean heads with isopropyl and foam swabs, never cotton. Replace drive belts; re-lubricate rails sparingly. Bake sticky-shed tapes (50–55 C, 8+ hours) before playing. Never force a shutter; transplant disks to donor jackets if needed. KryoFlux or Greaseweazle imaging before any repair attempts on precious originals.

Restoration order for a Greaseweazle Controller: 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision. Never power an unrestored electrical storage media record without a current-limited bring-up.
